query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, small, controlled changes in Al content change the atomic size mismatch and associated mixing enthalpy, which in turn govern the stability of the fcc solid solution. This mechanism controls the phase boundaries (e.g., onset of secondary phases or polymorphic transitions) that underlie the desirable high-temperature strength, radiation/environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy (HEA) exhibiting a single-phase fcc structure with established high-temperature and cryogenic mechanical properties.
generation.intervention: Controlled-variable compositional tuning by systematically varying the Al content (increases and decreases relative to the equiatomic composition) while holding the other elemental concentrations constant.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmospheres, spanning a wide temperature range (from cryogenic ~77 K to high temperatures >1000 K) with in-situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction, and incorporating simulated radiation and environmental stress exposures.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and phase fractions as measured by shifts in unit cell parameters and the appearance or suppression of secondary phases (e.g., fcc to hcp transitions) detected by in-situ XRD.
generation.mechanism: The key mechanism is that tuning the Al content alters the atomic size mismatch and, consequently, the mixing enthalpy among the constituent atoms. An increased Al content induces greater lattice distortion and a more negative mixing enthalpy, which can stabilize (or destabilize) the fcc phase depending on temperature and environmental conditions. This mediation of thermodynamic driving forces shifts the phase stability boundaries that directly affect high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic baseline, alloys with a modestly increased or decreased Al content will exhibit systematic shifts in their phase transformation temperatures (or phase fractions) as detected by in-situ XRD. These shifts will correlate with changes in mechanical properties – for example, altered yield strength at high temperatures and modifications in ductility and toughness at cryogenic temperatures – thus supporting the role of atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy in governing phase stability.
generation.baseline: The conventional equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with its known fcc structure and established balance of mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within a modest compositional variation window where other compositional or processing-induced effects (such as unwanted elemental segregation) are minimal; extreme deviations in Al content or processing conditions may invoke additional mechanisms not captured by this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between Al content variation and the temperature (or environmental) dependent phase stability is not fully defined. Also, the interplay between radiation-induced defects and compositional tuning adds complexity which might not be entirely explained by atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy alone.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with systematically varied Al contents around the equiatomic composition. Conduct in-situ synchrotron XRD measurements while cycling the temperature from cryogenic (~77 K) to high (>1000 K) under controlled inert atmospheres, and perform mechanical testing (including cryogenic toughness and high-temperature strength) with simulated radiation exposure.
measurements: Phase fractions and unit cell parameter shifts (from in-situ XRD) as a function of Al content and temperature.
Critical phase transformation temperatures (e.g., onset of fcc to hcp transitions) for each composition.
Mechanical properties such as yield strength, ductility, and fracture toughness at both high and cryogenic temperatures.
Radiation damage indicators under simulated environmental stresses.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the Al content does not result in systematic and reproducible shifts in phase stability (i.e., no measurable changes in phase boundaries or transition temperatures) and if the corresponding mechanical properties (high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness) remain statistically unchanged relative to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis that atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy governed by Al content are the primary factors controlling phase stability will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: However, there is also a question of the role of high configurational entropy in these materials with respect to properties, particularly how such high-entropy alloys compare with other equiatomic multi-element systems. Here we examine a variant of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy in which two of the elements have been removed. The resulting CrCoNi alloy, an equiatomic ‘medium-entropy alloy' (MEA), has a single-phase, fcc crystal structure, whose uniaxial tensile properties have recently been reported. The experimental results (X-ray diffraction and backscattered electron, BSE, images) are consistent with the CrCoNi ternary phase diagrams, which indicate that the equiatomic composition is a single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. cited_evidence.text: The first objective of this research was to develop new VCrMnFeCoNi alloys for use in cryogenic applications. To achieve the chemical compositions of these alloys, a computational thermodynamic approach of a VCrMnFeCoNi six-component system was used, from which HEA compositions having a wide temperature range of an fcc single phase were obtained. This thermodynamic-approach-based alloy design was very effective in comparison with conventional alloying methods, that is, empirical and trial-and-error-based alloy design and property evaluation, which demand significant time and are expensive,. Vanadium was selected as a new candidate alloying element in the CrMnFeCoNi alloy system because it shows a wide single-phase solid-solution range on binary phase diagrams with most elements, including Cr, Fe and Mn. Although most HEAs have equi-atomic or near-equi-atomic compositions, the equi-atomic composition is not believed to be the optimum composition for a wide range of materials properties. The CrMnFeCoNi alloy system is not a unique system that yields fcc-single-phase microstructures containing more than five components,,,,,. chosen.conditions: A direct comparison between the conventional equiatomic HEA (baseline) and modified alloys with a controlled increase or decrease in a key component (such as Al) under inert atmospheres, spanning temperature ranges from cryogenic (~77 K) to high temperatures (>1000 K) and with controlled radiation or environmental exposures
chosen.why: This move most directly fills the niche by proposing a mechanistic hypothesis that phase stability arises from the interplay between mixing enthalpy and entropy—specifically, by tuning the atomic size mismatch through controlled compositional changes. The approach employs standard materials-science techniques to isolate the effect of composition on phase boundaries, thus providing testable predictions. Observations such as systematic shifts in phase fractions or transition temperatures relative to the baseline would support the hypothesis, while a lack of such shifts would falsify it.
